The banana plant is
not a tree at all.
And that fact explains
why the banana you
eat is nearly identical
to almost every other one.
Despite growing up to
twenty-five feet tall,
the banana plant contains
no woody tissue.
Botanically speaking, the
banana plant is the
world's largest perennial
herb.
What appears to be
a solid tree trunk
is actually a "pseudostem"—a
false trunk formed by
tightly packed, overlapping
leaf sheaths wrapped around
each other like layers
of an onion.
The true heart of
the banana plant lives
entirely underground.
It is an enormous,
bulbous underground stem
called a rhizome, or corm.
This subterranean engine
stores nutrients and energy,
and it lets the
plant reproduce without seeds.
From the sides of
this underground corm,
the plant continuously
pushes out miniature genetic
duplicates—lateral shoots
commonly known as "suckers"
or "pups."
When a mature banana
stalk produces its massive
bunch of fruit,
that specific stalk dies off.
But before it withers,
several suckers have already
emerged from the root
system below.
Ancient farmers realized
that if they carefully
severed one of these
baby suckers from the
mother root and buried
it in fertile soil
elsewhere, it would rapidly
take root, sprout massive
leaves, and grow into
a full-sized, fruit-bearing
plant in roughly a year.
This technique is called
vegetative propagation.
Today, growers also use
micropropagation, commonly
known as plant tissue culture.
Scientists take microscopic
tissue samples from the
growing tip of a
high-yielding banana plant,
sanitize them to eliminate
pathogens, and place them
into sterile petri dishes
filled with agar and
specific growth hormones.
From a microscopic speck
of tissue, thousands of
identical, disease-free
clones can be manufactured
simultaneously.
Think about what that
means: almost every banana
you have ever bought
from a supermarket is
a clone of every other one.
They are not siblings;
they are identical twins
separated only by geography
and time.
Millions upon millions
of Cavendish plants
stretching across South
America, Africa, and Asia
share essentially the same
DNA.
Seeds were never required.
Only hands.
